title: India's UPI Reaches 10 Countries as Diaspora Emerges as Key Driver of Global Payments Push
excerpt: From Greece to the Gulf, India's homegrown payment system is expanding rapidly — and the 32-million-strong diaspora is at the center of the strategy.
body:
• India's Unified Payments Interface is now accepted in 10 countries after Greece went live in June 2026, with negotiations underway for 7–8 more markets.
  • A new India Post–UPU partnership connects UPI to 190+ national postal operators worldwide, targeting low-cost remittances for overseas Indians.
  • India received over $137.7 billion in remittances in 2024 — the largest in the world — and UPI's expansion could slash transfer costs from over 6% to as low as 2%.
  • The RBI and European Central Bank are in the "realisation phase" of linking UPI with Europe's TIPS instant payments system, potentially opening the continent's largest diaspora corridor.

India's Unified Payments Interface crossed a milestone in late June when Greece became the tenth country to accept UPI-based transactions. Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal witnessed a live demonstration at Eurobank's Athens headquarters, where the Greek lender partnered with NPCI International Payments Limited to enable instant, low-cost cross-border transfers for Indian residents and students in Greece.

The launch extended UPI's footprint into the European Union for the second time — after France — and underscored a broader strategy in which the Indian diaspora is not merely a beneficiary of global expansion but its primary commercial justification.

Ten Countries and Counting

UPI is now operational in Greece, Singapore, the UAE, France, Mauritius, Nepal, Bhutan, Qatar, Sri Lanka, and Cambodia. Each rollout follows a tailored model: bank-to-network partnerships, merchant QR code acceptance, or dedicated remittance corridors. Singapore's UPI-PayNow link, operational since 2023, remains the most mature integration, enabling peer-to-peer transfers in both directions.

Financial Services Secretary M. Nagaraju confirmed in late 2025 that India is in structured negotiations with 7–8 additional countries, primarily in East Asia and the Gulf. India has also joined Project Nexus alongside Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore, and Thailand — a multilateral initiative to connect domestic payment systems for instant cross-border retail payments.

"We have already expanded UPI services to a few countries, and more will be added soon, especially in East Asia."

— M. Nagaraju, Financial Services Secretary, Government of India

The Remittance Equation

India received over $137.7 billion in remittances in 2024, the largest volume of any country. For the diaspora, cross-border transfer costs remain a persistent friction. The World Bank estimates that international remittance fees often exceed 6% per transaction — a substantial burden on the millions of overseas workers, students, and professionals who send money home regularly.

UPI's architecture offers a structural alternative. The Kuwait–India corridor already recorded transaction costs of 2.1% in Q4 2024, well below the G20's benchmark of 3% by 2030. In Bahrain, home to approximately 320,000 Indians, the UPI–Fawri+ corridor promises to cut average remittance charges of ₹300–700 and reduce settlement times from days to seconds.

A parallel initiative could extend that cost advantage globally. India Post has partnered with the Universal Postal Union and NPCI International to connect UPI to the UPU's Interconnection Platform, linking more than 190 national postal operators worldwide. Under the system, funds sent from abroad can be collected at Indian post offices or credited directly to any UPI-linked bank account.

"With the UPU–India Post–UPI integration, clients of the posts at origin can credit accounts of anybody owning an account in India. Payments at destination are now made in cash by India Post or directly on account by UPI."

— David Avsec, Products and Account Relationships Coordinator, UPU Postal Technology Centre

Europe: The Next Frontier

The Reserve Bank of India and the European Central Bank are in what officials describe as the "realisation phase" of linking UPI with TIPS, Europe's instant payments system. If completed, the integration would open UPI corridors across the eurozone — a region home to hundreds of thousands of Indian students and professionals.

Greece's June launch and earlier rollouts in France, including at the Eiffel Tower in Paris and a department store in Nice, signal a focused push into European markets. Minister Goyal tied the payments expansion to the potential of an India-EU free trade agreement, framing UPI acceptance as both economic infrastructure and diplomatic leverage.

What It Means for NRIs

For the Indian diaspora, UPI's global expansion has immediate practical implications. NRIs in UPI-enabled countries can send money home faster and cheaper than through traditional banking channels. Apps like PhonePe and Paytm have added international UPI modes that allow merchant payments abroad and, in Singapore, peer-to-peer transfers — with PhonePe enabling inbound international payments for the first time.

At home, India's UPI processes over 21 billion transactions per month, accounting for 48.5% of the world's real-time payments. The system's domestic scale gives it credibility abroad, but the real test lies in building the kind of broad merchant acceptance and regulatory interoperability that turns a payments rail into everyday infrastructure.

What's Next

India's stated target is 12 or more fully connected countries by end of 2026, with a longer-term vision of 20-plus UPI-enabled markets. The India Post–UPU pilot is onboarding its first sending countries, and East Asian negotiations are advancing. But challenges remain: differing regulations, data-protection frameworks, and entrenched competition from Visa, Mastercard, and regional payment networks will test whether UPI can move beyond niche remittance corridors to genuine global acceptance.

For India's diaspora — the estimated 32 million people living and working abroad who collectively power the world's largest remittance flow — the stakes are straightforward: every new UPI corridor means less money lost to transfer fees and fewer days waiting for funds to arrive.
nri_angle: UPI's global expansion directly benefits NRIs by slashing remittance costs and enabling instant cross-border payments in countries where millions of Indians live, work, and study.
